clinicalPearls: Uncommon autosomal recessive congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by variants in HSD3B2, the type 2 isoenzyme expressed in adrenal cortex and gonads.
The enzyme converts delta-5 steroids to delta-4 steroids, so its loss blocks synthesis of cortisol, aldosterone and potent androgens simultaneously.
Delta-5 precursors, especially 17-hydroxypregnenolone and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), accumulate proximal to the block.
The severe classic form presents in the newborn period with salt-wasting adrenal crisis due to combined gluco- and mineralocorticoid deficiency.
46,XY infants are typically undervirilised because the weak androgen DHEA cannot fully masculinise the external genitalia.
46,XX infants may show mild clitoromegaly from peripheral conversion of the large excess of DHEA to active androgens.
A markedly elevated ratio of delta-5 to delta-4 steroids (for example 17-hydroxypregnenolone to 17-hydroxyprogesterone) is the biochemical hallmark.
Deficiency of the type 1 isoenzyme (peripheral tissues and placenta) does not cause this disorder, so the type 2 gene must be specifically implicated.
reference.pathophysiology: 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in HSD3B2, encoding the enzyme that catalyses the conversion of delta-5-3-beta-hydroxysteroids to delta-4-3-ketosteroids within the adrenal cortex and gonads. This step is common to the mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid and sex-steroid pathways, so its impairment blocks conversion of pregnenolone to progesterone, 17-hydroxypregnenolone to 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone to androstenedione. The result is deficient synthesis of aldosterone, cortisol and biologically potent androgens, with accumulation of the delta-5 precursors upstream of the block. Cortisol deficiency releases the pituitary from negative feedback and raises corticotrophin, driving adrenal hyperplasia and further precursor accumulation. Mineralocorticoid deficiency produces salt wasting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypovolaemia. In 46,XY fetuses the gonadal block prevents adequate androgen production, causing incomplete masculinisation, whereas in 46,XX fetuses the large excess of dehydroepiandrosterone can be converted peripherally by the intact type 1 isoenzyme into active androgens sufficient to cause mild virilisation. The distinctive biochemical signature is a raised ratio of delta-5 to delta-4 steroids, reflecting the specific enzymatic step that is impaired.
additionalDifferentials: Lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia and P450 side-chain cleavage deficiency

Non-classic 3-beta-HSD deficiency presenting with hyperandrogenism (a contested entity)
additionalInvestigations: Ratio of delta-5 to delta-4 steroids, ideally after ACTH stimulation
Serum electrolytes for hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone to confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency
Karyotype and genital/pelvic imaging in infants with atypical genitalia
redFlags: Neonatal salt-wasting adrenal crisis with hypovolaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia
Failure to thrive, poor feeding and vomiting in early infancy
Ambiguous or undervirilised genitalia requiring urgent multidisciplinary assessment
Circulatory collapse or arrhythmia from severe electrolyte derangement
Intercurrent illness precipitating decompensation in a known case
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition of adrenal crisis, glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement, salt supplementation in infancy and sex-steroid support as needed, survival and development are generally good. Prognosis is compromised by delayed diagnosis and unrecognised salt-wasting crises, and long-term care must address growth, puberty and fertility as well as the associated disorder of sex development.
pitfalls: Measuring only 17-hydroxyprogesterone and missing the diagnosis, since it can be normal or only mildly raised; the delta-5 precursors are the key markers.
Confusing mild 46,XX virilisation with 21-hydroxylase deficiency without checking the delta-5 to delta-4 ratio.
Failing to appreciate that both salt wasting and undervirilisation of a 46,XY infant can coexist.
Overlooking the risk of life-threatening crisis during minor illness in an inadequately replaced child.
Attributing the disorder to the ubiquitous type 1 isoenzyme rather than the adrenal/gonadal type 2 enzyme.

management: Lifelong glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone to correct cortisol deficiency and suppress the excess corticotrophin drive.
Mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone plus sodium chloride supplementation in infancy to control salt-wasting.
Sex-steroid support at the expected age of puberty, with individualised management of atypical genitalia guided by karyotype and gender identity.
Stress dosing of glucocorticoid during intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma, with a written sick-day plan and injectable hydrocortisone for emergencies.
Immediate treatment of salt-wasting adrenal crisis with parenteral hydrocortisone and intravenous saline with dextrose for accompanying hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia.
Regular monitoring of growth, electrolytes, plasma renin activity and delta-5 steroid precursors, with bone-age assessment.
Multidisciplinary care through paediatric endocrinology, urology and psychology, with genetic counselling and carrier testing for this autosomal recessive disorder.
